how: One source mutation applied to the working tree, the named suite run against it, then the file restored before the next row (X14/X15's convention: `before` is the shipped source the row was run against and `after` the text that replaced it). Device rows ran on lease G27-ul745, pair-b (`iPhone Air` / iOS 27 and emulator-5570 / API 35, Metro 8293); the filtered gate names satisfy nothing but their own name. Row 1 needs no device (JVM), row 2 no device (jest), rows 3-5 share one mutated Android build, rows 6-7 share one mutated iOS build. Logs: `gate.mjs logs --branch task/G27-search-field-keyboard`.

mutations.mutation: the editor-info decode reads the variation before the class, the mistake an earlier cut of this function made
mutations.before:
fun nameOfInputType(inputType: Int): String =
    when (inputType and android.text.InputType.TYPE_MASK_CLASS) {
mutations.note: TYPE_NUMBER_VARIATION_PASSWORD and TYPE_TEXT_VARIATION_URI are the same bit, so a secure number pad decoded by variation alone is a URL keyboard. The second row names the bit, which is why the fixture is not allowed to coincide with a plausible fallback.

mutations.mutation: the editor record is scraped where the manager keeps it — an older cut of this reader, before it was run on a device
redTests: imeEditorInfo reads the keyboard and the action key off the IME service section: expect(received).not.toBeNull() — Received: null (scripts/__tests__/real-input-ime-frame.test.js:161)
mutations.note: The organic kind: this is the bug the first device run showed, in the shape of a red unit test rather than an 11-minute gate. `dumpsys input_method` is the manager's dump and prints the editor record only in proto; its text dump forwards to the bound IME, which prints `mInputEditorInfo:` and `EditorInfo.dump()`.

mutations.mutation: MUTATION A — the field is handed what v1 effectively handed it, so the three props move the model and nothing else

mutations.mutation: MUTATION A (the same build as the harness row)
mutations.run: real-input:android:--control:search-field — FAIL, 2 checks of the section
redTests: keyboardType="number-pad" reaches the IME as a number keyboard, Search key included — expected class=number variation=0x0 flags=none action=search, saw class=text variation=0x0 flags=auto-correct action=search

keyboardType="email-address" with autoCorrect={false} reaches the IME as an email keyboard that refuses autocorrection, Search key included — expected class=text variation=0x20 flags=none action=search, saw class=text variation=0x0 flags=auto-correct action=search
mutations.note: Both red lines are the IME's own record of the connection, and the section's first check — a field with no keyboard prop still asking for the text keyboard, autocorrected, with the Search key — stayed green under the mutation, which is the half that says v1's defaults survived. The keys reaching the field and the Search key submitting also stayed green: the mutation moves the keyboard, not the field.

mutations.mutation: MUTATION B — the keyboard is the one thing that survives the pool: `reset()` keeps the previous owner's three values
mutations.after:
val keptKeyboard = model.keyboardType
    val keptCapitalisation = model.autoCapitalize
    val keptAutoCorrect = model.autoCorrect
    …
    model.keyboardType = keptKeyboard (and the other two)
mutations.note: Recorded because it is a hole, not a proof: with every prop always passed (D7b), the second owner's own keyboard props are applied on mount, so the recycled field is correct whatever `reset()` does. The recycle assertions in the harness therefore document the invariant rather than prove the reset. Closing it needs a read taken between `reset()` and the first prop write, which the harness cannot ask for from JS.

mutations.mutation: MUTATION C — the keyboard trait is the one this component used to fix, so it is the one the props may not move
mutations.before: if keyboardType != traits.keyboard { keyboardType = traits.keyboard; traitsChanged = true }
mutations.after:
let appliedKeyboard: UIKeyboardType = .default
    if keyboardType != appliedKeyboard { keyboardType = appliedKeyboard; traitsChanged = true }
redTests: SearchField gives the field the keyboard the app asked for, Search key included: SearchField keyboard: a focused field to reload its own keyboard never happened; last report {"focused":true,"keyboardType":"default","autoCapitalize":"none","autoCorrect":true,"returnKeyType":"search"}
mutations.note: iOS answers a keyboard change while the keyboard is up, so this is the first place the trait is asked for; the mutation leaves the other two props alone, and they read back as asked in the same report — which is what isolates the finding to the keyboard trait.
